cultivar: Bangdong large-leaf population (Yunnan assamica), old trees kept in the local 'vine' (tengtiao) pruning style
processing: Raw pu-erh: pan-fired, rolled and sun-dried maocha pressed into cakes or sold loose; the trees are pruned so that only the tip shoots grow, giving long, thin, dark leaves.
harvest_season: Spring (late March to April); autumn tea exists but the premium is all about spring old-tree leaf.
appearance_dry: Long, slender, dark and tightly twisted leaves with thin stems and relatively few buds, pressed loosely.
appearance_liquor: Deep bright gold, thick-looking and clear.
appearance_wet: Long, narrow, dark olive leaves with the whippy stems of vine-pruned trees.
taste_profile: Intensely aromatic, with ripe fruit, orchid and honey, a thick heavy body, a measured bitterness that turns quickly, and a strong, cooling returning sweetness; more powerful than Bingdao, more fragrant than Lao Ban Zhang.

brewing.notes: Rinse once, quickly. The thin vine-style leaves open fast, so flash the early steeps; strong enough that 6–7 g is plenty.

vintage_note: Sold by spring harvest year and by garden on Mangluo mountain, mostly as loose maocha and small-run cakes. Xigui became a famous name a little before Bingdao, around 2008–2010, so a handful of mid-aged lots (roughly 2010–2016) circulate among collectors, but the great majority of what is sold is young tea from 2015–2025 and there is no aged Xigui market to speak of. It is drunk young for its aroma and bought in dry storage; the Bangdong area produces far more tea than the Xigui gardens can, which is where most 'Xigui' comes from.
description:
Xigui is a small village on the bank of the Lancang (Mekong) river in Bangdong township, Lincang, with its best gardens on Mangluo mountain at only 750–1,000 m, far lower than most famous pu-erh origins. People call it the Lao Ban Zhang of Lincang: aromatic, heavy and strong, and priced accordingly, with Bingdao as the sweet counterpart.

The trees are old but kept in the local 'tengtiao' or vine style, where side shoots and mature leaves are stripped so the energy goes into long whippy tips; the maocha is therefore dark, slender and bud-poor, and looks nothing like a fat Bingdao leaf. Processing is normal sheng, pan-fired, rolled and sun-dried, and because the leaf is thin it rolls tight and releases quickly in the cup.

Young Xigui is big: ripe fruit and orchid on the nose, a dense and almost chewy body, a controlled bitterness that turns into sweetness within seconds and a cooling finish that lasts. It sits between Lao Ban Zhang's weight and Bingdao's sugar, which is why Lincang people rank it as their top tea. It brews for a very long session; the only way to spoil it is to overleaf and oversteep early, when the bitterness overruns the fruit.

Sold by spring year and garden, mainly as maocha or small cakes from boutique brands. Real Xigui is a tiny amount of tea from one hillside, and Bangdong township around it makes a great deal of similar-looking vine-style tea, so the label 'Xigui' is at best a style guarantee at most prices. Long thin dark leaves are the right look, but the real test is whether the aroma and thickness match the ambition on the wrapper.

For the same style at a fair price, buy Bangdong tea sold as Bangdong; it shares the aromatics and much of the body.
sources_note: Elevation of the Mangluo gardens is usually given as roughly 750–1,000 m; the year Xigui prices took off is given variously as 2008–2010.
history:
Xigui is a small village by the Lancang river in Bangdong township, Lincang, and its tea takes its name from the place. Its gardens on Mangluo mountain lie unusually low for a famous pu-erh origin.

Its fame among drinkers is fairly recent, part of the wave of interest in single-village Lincang tea, and it now ranks with Bingdao among the area's expensive names. Little is documented about its earlier history, and the tea sold under the name far exceeds what one hillside could plausibly give.
